title: Programs & Knob Control
blurb: Save one setup for PadLab and another for your DAW, so switching between practice and production is a single button press.

steps.title: What a program actually stores
body: A program is a saved snapshot of the controller's assignments: which note each pad sends on each bank, which CC each knob sends, and the MIDI channel everything goes out on.
It does not store any sound. The sound always comes from whatever is receiving the MIDI — PadLab's synthesized kit, or a plugin in your DAW.
Press PROG SELECT to see the saved programs and step between them.
This is why the same pad can play a kick in PadLab and open a totally different instrument in your DAW: only the assignments changed.
steps.checkpoint: You can move between programs and see the display change, with no change in what the pads sound like in PadLab.
steps.tip: If your unit's programs are edited in Akai's MPK Mini editor rather than on the display, do the same steps there — the concepts are identical.

steps.title: Make a practice program
body: Start from the factory program and change as little as possible: PadLab's built-in profile expects the factory pad notes, so leaving them alone means it works with no setup.
Set the MIDI channel to one your other gear is not listening on, so practising does not trigger a synth in the next room.
Save it to a program slot and name it for what it is.
Now open PadLab, check the device chip reads your controller, and play a pad on each bank to confirm nothing moved.
steps.checkpoint: Recalling your practice program leaves every pad landing where PadLab expects it.
steps.tip: If you have already run MIDI Learn in PadLab, that mapping wins regardless of what the controller sends — but keep the program clean anyway, so the app works on a machine where you have not.

steps.title: Assign the knobs to something useful
body: Each knob sends a CC number on a channel. The receiving software decides what that CC does.
Pick a CC for each knob and write the numbers down. Unlabelled knobs are the reason most controllers end up with three unused ones.
Set the range where it matters: a filter knob that only sweeps the useful half of its travel is far more playable than one that spends most of its range doing nothing.
Save the program again once the knobs are how you want them.
steps.checkpoint: Every knob moves something you actually use, and you know which CC each one sends.
steps.tip: PadLab ignores knobs entirely — a learned mapping only listens to your pads. Knob assignments are for your DAW; they cannot disturb a lesson.

steps.title: One program per context
body: Build a second program for production: your DAW's drum-rack note layout, knobs mapped to the mixer or a plugin, and whatever channel your template expects.
Keep the practice program on a slot you can find by feel, so a warm-up never turns into a ten-minute setup detour.
Switching contexts is then one button press in each direction.
Check both programs after a firmware update — that is the one time saved assignments tend to move.
steps.checkpoint: You can go from a PadLab lesson to your DAW session and back without re-mapping anything.
steps.tip: Back up your programs with the editor software if yours supports it. Rebuilding a knob map from memory is an hour you will not enjoy.
